# inventory

## `lookup.loan_borrowers(loans, members)`

Pair every loan with the borrower's name.

Returns `(order id, customer name)` for every order in `loans` whose `customer_id` matches the `id` of a record in `members`, in order of `loans`; orders without a matching customer are left out; if several customers share an id the first one counts.

The items are hashable and compare with `==`; the lists can hold tens of thousands of entries, so the cost of a call has to grow about linearly with their size.

## `reports.duplicate_scans(scans)`

Barcodes that were scanned more than once.

Returns the items that occur more than once in `scans`, each once, in the order of their first occurrence.

The items are hashable and compare with `==`; the lists can hold tens of thousands of entries, so the cost of a call has to grow about linearly with their size.

I have a counting harness that compares the number of comparisons and hash operations against the input size, so a constant-factor tweak will not be enough.

## `scan.tidy_catalogue(skus)`

Summarise a catalogue feed: the distinct SKUs and the ones that were listed several times.

Returns `unique` (the items of `skus` without repeats, in order of first appearance) and `repeats` (those unique items that occur more than once).

The items are hashable and compare with `==`; the lists can hold tens of thousands of entries, so the cost of a call has to grow about linearly with their size.

## `batch.slot_numbers(shelf, requests)`

Shelf slot of every requested book (-1 when it is not on the shelf).

For every item of `requests` returns the index of its first occurrence in `shelf`, or -1 when it does not occur; the result has one entry per item of `requests`, in order.

The items are hashable and compare with `==`; the lists can hold tens of thousands of entries, so the cost of a call has to grow about linearly with their size.

## `reports.compare_inventory(expected, counted)`

Compare the expected stock ids with the ids found in the stock take.

Compares two lists of ids: `matched` are the ids of `expected` that also occur in `counted`, `missing` those of `expected` that do not, `extra` those of `counted` that do not occur in `expected`; every list keeps the order (and repeats) of its source.

The items are hashable and compare with `==`; the lists can hold tens of thousands of entries, so the cost of a call has to grow about linearly with their size.
